pairs.source_text: Hospes, quod deico paullum est, asta ac pellege.
pairs.question: Quo vocabulo celeberrimum Claudiae elogium sepulcrale eum qui praeterit statim compellat?
pairs.question_en: With what word of address does the most famous epitaph of Claudia immediately hail the passer-by?
pairs.derivation: Opening word of the most famous Roman epitaph, the elogium of Claudia (CLE 52 = CIL 1.1211), anthologized in every Latin reader. 'Hospes' is the classic epigraphic address to the passer-by (so too B 53, 838, 1532). Anchored to the named celebrated text; single verifiable answer (the poem's first word). Criterion 8 holds because the famous poem's content, not an obscure person, carries the fact.

pairs.source_text: Suom mareitum corde deilexit souo.
pairs.question: Quem Claudia, ut eius elogium celeberrimum testatur, corde suo dilexit?
pairs.question_en: Whom, as her most famous epitaph attests, did Claudia love with her whole heart?
pairs.derivation: Content fact of the celebrated Claudia elogium: she loved her husband with her heart. Anchored to Claudia's famous epitaph; single answer supported verbatim by 'Suom mareitum corde deilexit souo' (archaic spelling of suum maritum ... suo). Ambient knowledge for Latin readers because the poem is a stock anthology piece.

pairs.source_text: Gnatos duos creauit.
pairs.question: Quot filios Claudia, cuius elogium sepulcrale celeberrimum est, peperit?
pairs.question_en: How many sons did Claudia, whose funeral elogium is most famous, bear?
pairs.derivation: Number fact of the celebrated Claudia elogium: 'Gnatos duos creauit' (gnatos = natos). Anchored to the famous named text; single number answer, supported verbatim. Closed-book for anyone who knows the anthologized poem.

pairs.source_text: Gnatos duos creauit. Horum alterum in terra linquit, alium sub terra locat.
pairs.question: Quot ex duobus filiis suis Claudia moriens in terra superstites reliquit?
pairs.question_en: How many of her two sons did the dying Claudia leave surviving on earth?
pairs.derivation: The famous antithesis of the Claudia elogium: of her two sons she leaves one on the earth and places the other beneath it, i.e. one son survived her and one predeceased her. Anchored to Claudia's celebrated epitaph; single number answer supported verbatim ('Horum alterum in terra linquit, alium sub terra locat').

pairs.source_text: Domum servavit. Lanam fecit.
pairs.question: Quae duo officia domestica in celeberrimo Claudiae elogio laudantur?
pairs.question_en: Which two domestic duties are praised in the most famous elogium of Claudia?
pairs.answer_en: She kept the house and worked wool.
pairs.derivation: The most quoted line of Roman funerary epigraphy: 'Domum servavit. Lanam fecit.' — the two canonical virtues of the Roman matrona (housekeeping and wool-working, cf. the lanifica ideal). Anchored to the famous Claudia elogium; the paired answer is stated verbatim. Quintessential criterion-8 material: the matron ideal is shared Roman culture, and this poem is its textbook attestation.

pairs.source_text: Dixi. Abei.
pairs.question: Quo verbo extremo Claudiae elogium hospitem dimittit?
pairs.question_en: With what final word does the elogium of Claudia dismiss the passer-by?
pairs.answer_en: 'Go' (abi; on the stone in archaic spelling 'abei').
pairs.derivation: The famously abrupt close of the Claudia elogium: 'Dixi. Abei.' — 'I have spoken. Go.' The final word is abi in its archaic spelling abei; the answer normalizes the spelling of the same word. Anchored to the celebrated named text; single verifiable answer; the brusque dismissal is one of the poem's most remembered features and survives translation.

pairs.source_text: tantum est. hoc voluit nescius ne esses. vale.
pairs.question: Qua brevi formula tituli sepulcrales Romani significant nihil iam restare quod legatur?
pairs.question_en: With what brief formula do Roman epitaphs signal that nothing more remains to be read?
pairs.derivation: The laconic closing formula of Roman epitaphs, attested here on the stone of the praeco Olus Granius: 'tantum est' — that is all — followed by the farewell 'vale'. Convention-level fact of the epigraphic genre (the individual named on the stone is deliberately not asked about); the formula itself is what a reader of Roman inscriptions carries. Supported verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Mi fili, mater rogat ut me ad te recipias.
pairs.question: Quid mater orba in titulis sepulcralibus Romanis filium mortuum rogare solet?
pairs.question_en: What does a bereaved mother, in Roman epitaphs, customarily ask of her dead son?
pairs.answer_en: That he receive her (to himself, among the dead).
pairs.derivation: The touching formula of bereaved parents asking the dead child to 'receive' them when they die: 'mater rogat ut me ad te recipias', attested twice in this collection (B 151 and B 1892 'mater tua rogat te ut se ad te recipias'). A recognized, much-anthologized convention of Roman funerary culture, not the detail of one household; short indirect-command answer with indirect reflexive se referring to the mother.

pairs.source_text: vive dum vivis, nec quidquam denegaveris animo indulgere, quem commodavit deus.
pairs.question: Qua brevi sententia carmina sepulcralia Romana convivalia monent praesenti vita fruendum esse?
pairs.question_en: With what brief maxim do Roman convivial epitaphs advise that one must enjoy life while one has it?
pairs.derivation: The proverbial carpe-diem motto of the convivial epitaph, stated verbatim in this banquet poem ('Adeste amici...'). A famous saying whose wording is itself the checkable fact; convention-level, so criterion 8 holds via the shared formula rather than any individual. Translatable as a maxim.

pairs.source_text: Dum vixi, bibi libenter. bibite vos, qui vivitis!
pairs.question: Quid tituli sepulcrales convivales Romani eos qui vivunt facere iubent?
pairs.question_en: What do the convivial Roman epitaphs bid those who are alive to do?
pairs.derivation: The drinking exhortation of the convivial epitaph type: the dead man drank gladly while he lived and bids the living drink ('bibite vos, qui vivitis'), corroborated in this collection by B 190 ('Baccho madentes') and B 1500 ('Es, bibe, lude, veni'). A celebrated genre convention of Roman funerary culture; single short answer supported verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Quod edi bibi, mecum habeo, quod reliqui, perdidi.
pairs.question: Secundum notissimam sententiam sepulcralem 'Quod edi bibi, mecum habeo', quid mortuus perdidit?
pairs.question_en: According to the famous epitaph maxim 'What I ate and drank I have with me', what has the dead man lost?
pairs.derivation: The celebrated Epicurean tomb maxim (the 'Sardanapalus' sentiment known already to Cicero, Tusc. 5.101): only what one has eaten and drunk remains one's own; what one left behind is lost. The completion of the famous saying is the checkable fact; anchored by quoting its well-known opening; supported verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Qui legis hunc titulum, mortalem te esse memento.
pairs.question: Quid tituli sepulcrales Romani eum qui legit meminisse iubent?
pairs.question_en: What do Roman epitaphs bid their reader remember?
pairs.derivation: The memento-mori formula of Roman epitaphs, stated verbatim: 'mortalem te esse memento', echoed in this collection by B 83 ('hoc est veniundum tibi') and B 799. One of the most famous conventions of Roman funerary (and triumphal) culture; convention-level anchoring to the genre of tituli sepulcrales; short indirect-statement answer.

pairs.source_text: Debita libertas iuveni mihi lege negata morte immatura reddita perpetua est.
pairs.question: Quid mors, ut in titulis sepulcralibus servorum Romanorum legitur, servis tandem perpetuum dedit?
pairs.question_en: What, as one reads in the epitaphs of Roman slaves, did death at last give slaves in perpetuity?
pairs.derivation: The distinctively Roman slave-epitaph topos: death confers the freedom life (and law) denied — 'debita libertas ... morte ... reddita perpetua est', corroborated by B 1331 ('nunc mors perpetua libertatem dedit'). Rooted in the Roman institutions of slavery and manumission, so culturally salient at the level of shared custom, not of the anonymous individual; single short answer supported verbatim.

pairs.source_text: quisque huic tumulo possuit ardente lucernam, illius cineres aurea terra tegat.
pairs.question: Quod munus ardens ad tumulos mortuorum ponere Romani pii solebant?
pairs.question_en: What burning offering did dutiful Romans customarily place at the tombs of the dead?
pairs.derivation: The custom of placing a lit lamp (lucerna) at the tomb, attested by this epitaph's reciprocal blessing on whoever sets one there ('quisque huic tumulo possuit ardente lucernam'). Grave lamps are a staple of Roman funerary cult and archaeology — ambient cultural knowledge; the stone's obscure Septima is not the subject. Single-word answer supported verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Tu qui carpis iter gressu properante, viator, siste gradum, quaeso. quod peto, parva mora est.
pairs.question: Quid tituli sepulcrales Romani a viatore gressu properante primum petere solent?
pairs.question_en: What do Roman epitaphs customarily first ask of the hurrying traveler?
pairs.derivation: The proverbial 'siste, viator' convention: the tomb by the roadside asks the passer-by to stop (and then read), promising only a small delay. Attested verbatim here ('siste gradum, quaeso') and throughout the collection (B 52 'asta ac pellege', B 53 'rogat ut resistas', B 848). A defining, famous convention of the genre; convention-level anchoring; short answer.

pairs.source_text: Dic rogo qui transis: sit tibi terra levis.
pairs.question: Quae verba fausta viator praeteriens mortuo dicere rogatur in titulis sepulcralibus Romanis?
pairs.question_en: What words of good omen is the passing traveler asked to say to the dead in Roman epitaphs?
pairs.answer_en: 'Sit tibi terra levis' ('may the earth lie light upon you').
pairs.derivation: The most famous of all Roman epitaph formulas, abbreviated S.T.T.L. on countless stones: the passer-by is asked to speak the wish that the earth lie light on the dead. Attested verbatim here and repeatedly in the collection (B 1194, 1269, 1308, 1497). Convention-level cultural knowledge par excellence; single fixed-formula answer.

pairs.source_text: Evasi effugi. Spes et Fortuna valete, nil mihi vobiscum est, ludificate alios.
pairs.question: Quibus deabus notissima formula sepulcralis 'Evasi, effugi' valedicit?
pairs.question_en: To which goddesses does the famous epitaph formula 'I have escaped, I have got away' bid farewell?
pairs.derivation: The celebrated 'Evasi, effugi' epigram (a Latin rendering of a famous Greek sepulchral couplet): the dead man bids farewell to Hope and Fortune and tells them to make sport of others. Anchored to the named famous formula and to the two named goddesses; two-name answer supported verbatim ('Spes et Fortuna valete').

pairs.source_text: vixit an. XV mensib. III dieb. XI hor. VII.
pairs.question: Praeter annos mensesque et dies, quas etiam partes temporis minores tituli sepulcrales Romani in aetate defunctorum nonnumquam enumerant?
pairs.question_en: Besides years, months, and days, what still smaller units of time do Roman epitaphs sometimes count in stating the age of the dead?
pairs.derivation: The 'vixit annos' age formula and its famous precision: Roman epitaphs count a life down to years, months, days, and even hours, as here ('vixit an. XV mensib. III dieb. XI hor. VII' — 15 years, 3 months, 11 days, 7 hours). A hallmark convention of Roman epigraphy noted in every handbook; convention-level anchoring (the girl Salvidiena herself is not asked about); single short answer supported verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Dis Manibus sacrum. memoriae aeternae C. Valeri Saturnini, qui vixit annis noviens denis, prope convenientibus annis.
pairs.question: Quibus numinibus tituli sepulcrales Romani, litteris D M notati, dedicari solent?
pairs.question_en: To which divinities are Roman tombstones, marked with the letters D M, customarily dedicated?
pairs.answer_en: To the Di Manes, the spirits of the dead.
pairs.derivation: The universal Roman dedication formula D(is) M(anibus): tombs are consecrated to the deified spirits of the dead, the Di Manes. Attested verbatim here ('Dis Manibus sacrum') and in B 439; cf. B 1269 'sacri sunt Manes'. The single most recognizable convention of Roman epigraphy — flagship criterion-8 material; fixed two-word answer.

pairs.source_text: Lecto merum profunde.
pairs.question: Quem liquorem viator ad sepulcrum mortui profundere in titulis Romanis iubetur?
pairs.question_en: What drink is the traveler bidden, in Roman epitaphs, to pour out at the tomb of the dead?
pairs.derivation: The rite of the wine libation to the dead: this epitaph closes by ordering the reader to pour unmixed wine on the burial couch ('Lecto merum profunde'), and B 838 likewise has the dead ask for a share of the drink ('misce bibe da mi'). Wine offerings at the tomb (as at the Parentalia) are ambient Roman religious custom; single-word answer supported verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Moneo te lectis litteris, ne contemnas et velis titulum movere, et corpori iniuriam facere. Si quis autem sibi admiserit, non bono suo fecerit, et superos et inferos iratos habeat.
pairs.question: Quos deos iratos habiturum esse tituli sepulcrales Romani eum minantur qui sepulcrum violaverit?
pairs.question_en: Which gods do Roman epitaphs threaten will be angry at anyone who violates the tomb?
pairs.answer_en: The gods above and the gods below.
pairs.derivation: The tomb-violation curse, a famous fixture of ancient epitaphs: whoever moves the stone or harms the body 'et superos et inferos iratos habeat' — will have both the gods above and the gods below against him; cf. B 838 and B 1532 ('noli ossa mea violare'). Convention-level religious fact of Roman funerary culture; paired answer supported verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Balnea vina Venus corrumpunt corpora nostra, set vitam faciunt balnea vina Venus.
pairs.question: Quae tria, ut celeberrimus titulus sepulcralis Romanus ait, corpora nostra corrumpunt sed vitam faciunt?
pairs.question_en: What three things, as a most famous Roman epitaph says, ruin our bodies but make life worth living?
pairs.derivation: The proverbial 'balnea vina Venus' epitaph, one of the most quoted of all Roman inscriptions: the three great pleasures of Roman life corrupt the body yet make life itself. Anchored to the celebrated saying; fixed three-item answer supported verbatim; the trio (baths, wine, love) is quintessential shared Roman culture and fully translatable.

pairs.source_text: Viator, viator! Quod tu es, ego fui; quod nunc sum, et tu eris
pairs.question: Quibus verbis pergit notissima formula sepulcralis quae incipit 'Quod tu es, ego fui'?
pairs.answer: Quod nunc sum, et tu eris.
pairs.question_en: With what words does the famous epitaph formula that begins 'What you are, I was' continue?
pairs.answer_en: 'What I am now, you too will be.'
pairs.derivation: The most famous memento-mori formula of the sepulchral tradition — 'quod tu es, ego fui; quod nunc sum, et tu eris' — addressed to the viator, with variants in this very collection (B 799 'fuimus quandoque quod estis'; CIL 8.9913 'Quod tu, et ego; quod ego, et omnes'). The completion of the celebrated saying is the checkable fact; supported verbatim; the maxim survives in many languages.
